title: Weather, nature & seasons
goal: Talk about the weather and seasons, describe the landscape, and say what the weather is going to do.
intro:
The Pashtun homeland is a land of contrasts: snowy peaks of the Hindu Kush and Safed Koh, green valleys like Swat, the hot plains of Jalalabad and Peshawar, and the deserts of the south around Kandahar. Weather is a constant topic — and a matter of life for farmers waiting for **باران** (rain) and **واوره** (snow), which fills the rivers in spring.

In this unit you'll learn nature and weather words, how Pashto talks about weather (often with the rain or snow as the subject), and how to say what's going to happen with **به**.

grammar.title: Talking about the weather
grammar.body:
English uses a dummy 'it' (it's raining, it's cold). Pashto doesn't — the weather itself is the subject:

**باران ورېږي** 'rain falls' = it's raining
**واوره ورېږي** 'snow falls' = it's snowing
**باد چلېږي** 'wind moves' = it's windy
**ګرمي ده / يخني ده** 'there is heat / cold' = it's hot / cold
**يخ دی** 'it is cold' (short and common)
**هوا ګرمه ده** 'the weather is hot' — هوا is feminine, so adjectives take -a: ښه، يخه، ګرمه.

For seasons, use **په … کې**: په ژمي کې 'in winter', په اوړي کې 'in summer' (the -ay ending becomes -i in the oblique).

examples.native: په کابل کې ژمی ډېر سوړ وي.
examples.roman: pə kābúl ke zhmay ḍer soṛ wi.
examples.en: Winter in Kabul is very cold. (وي = 'is' generally)

examples.native: په جلال اباد کې ژمی ګرم وي.
examples.roman: pə jalālābā́d ke zhmay garm wi.

examples.native: په اوړي کې په کندهار کې ډېره ګرمي وي.
examples.roman: pə oṛí ke pə kandahā́r ke ḍéra garmí wi.
examples.en: In summer it's very hot in Kandahar.
At night the stars are visible.

grammar.title: 'It's going to …': به + perfective
grammar.body:
To say what **will** or **is going to** happen, put the particle **به** (ba) before the verb, and use the **perfective** present (with و- or another perfective form):

باران **به** وشي 'it's going to rain' (lit. rain will happen)
واوره **به** وورېږي 'it will snow'

به is unstressed and usually comes right after the first word or phrase of the sentence, like the clitics. For 'will be' use **به … وي**: سبا به هوا ښه وي 'tomorrow the weather will be good'.

Notice also **وي** (wi): besides 'will be' after به, it is the 'general' form of 'to be' for things that are usually true: په ژمي کې يخ **وي** 'it's (always) cold in winter'.

examples.en: It looks like it's going to snow.
It's going to get hot now.
The wind will stop in the evening.

examples.native: په پسرلي کې به ګلان راشي.
examples.roman: pə psarlí ke ba gulā́n rā́shi.
examples.en: In spring the flowers will come out.

dialogue.title: A phone call between Kabul and Jalalabad
dialogue.setting: In January, Wahid in Kabul phones his sister Shabnam in Jalalabad.

lines.speaker: Wahid
lines.native: سلام خورې! هلته هوا څنګه ده؟
lines.roman: salā́m xóre! hálta hawā́ tsə́nga da?
lines.en: Hi sister! What's the weather like there?

lines.speaker: Shabnam
lines.native: ډېره ښه ده! لمر دی، هوا توده ده.
lines.roman: ḍéra ṣa da! lmar day, hawā́ tawdá da.
lines.en: Lovely! It's sunny and the weather's warm.

lines.speaker: Wahid
lines.native: دلته ډېر يخ دی. پرون ټوله ورځ واوره وورېده.
lines.roman: dálta ḍer yax day. parún ṭóla wradz wā́wra wə́wreda.
lines.en: It's very cold here. Yesterday it snowed all day.

lines.speaker: Wahid
lines.native: نه، خو ورېځې دي او باد چلېږي. ښکاري چې ماښام به بيا واوره وشي.
lines.roman: na, xo wredzé di aw bād chaléẓi. ṣkā́ri che māṣā́m ba biyā́ wā́wra wə́shi.
lines.en: No, but it's cloudy and windy. It looks like it'll snow again this evening.

lines.speaker: Shabnam
lines.native: نو جلال اباد ته راشه! دلته نارنج ګل کوي.
lines.roman: no jalālābā́d ta rā́sha! dálta nārə́nj gul kawí.
lines.en: Then come to Jalalabad! The bitter oranges are blossoming here.

lines.speaker: Wahid
lines.native: ډېر ښه! د جمعې په ورځ به درشم.
lines.roman: ḍer ṣə! də jumʿé pə wradz ba dárshəm.
lines.en: Great! I'll come to you on Friday.

lines.speaker: Shabnam
lines.native: ګرمې جامې مه راوړه، دلته اړتيا نشته!
lines.roman: gárme jā́me ma rāwṛá, dálta aṛtiyā́ nə́shta!
lines.en: Don't bring warm clothes — you won't need them here!

culture: Pashtun life follows the seasons. **Spring** (پسرلی) is celebrated in poetry and song as the season of love and flowers; in Jalalabad the orange blossom festival (د نارنج ګل) draws visitors, and in Afghanistan Nowruz picnics welcome the new year. **Summer** sends Peshawar and Kandahar families to the cool mountain valleys; **winter** brings heavy snow to Kabul and the high passes, when families gather around the **صندلي** (a low table over a charcoal brazier, covered with a quilt). Rain is a blessing in this dry region, and people often say د خدای رحمت دی 'it's God's mercy' when it rains.

tip.title: No 'it' in weather talk
tip.body:
- Pashto has no dummy 'it': the weather itself is the subject. ګرمي **ده** 'it's hot' (lit. heat is), يخ **دی** 'it's cold'.
- **هوا** is feminine, so its adjectives end in -a: هوا ګرم**ه** / يخ**ه** / تود**ه** ده.
- ډېر agrees too: ډېر**ه** ګرمي، ډېر يخ.

tip.title: 'Is going to': به + perfective
tip.body:
- Put **به** before the verb and use the perfective: باران **به** وشي 'it's going to rain'.
- به comes after the first word or phrase: سبا **به** …، نن **به** ….
- 'Will be' is **به … وي**: سبا به هوا ښه **وي**.
